purpose: Review a primary native-range diet study to complement foreign introduced-population evidence, while preserving the study's historical Japanese site, size and seasonal limits.

study.title: Ecology of the Japanese Loach, Misgurnus anguillicaudatus (Cantor) (II): Food Habit
study.citation: Kubota, Zenziro. (1961). Ecology of the Japanese Loach, Misgurnus anguillicaudatus (Cantor) (II): Food Habit. Journal of National Fisheries University, 11(1), 177-195.
study.researchPeriodAsReported: Gut-content fish were collected from 1958 to 1959; a separate feeding-preference experiment was conducted in May and September 1956.
study.studyLocation: Nagata River, Shimonoseki, Japan; the paper also describes a separate shallow mud-bottom pond experiment in Yoshimi-cho, Shimonoseki.
study.sampleScope: The gut-content methods describe fish 15-131 mm body length. No single total sample size is stated in the methods excerpt reviewed; tables organize observations by size class and date.
methodsAsReported: Fish collected in Nagata River were fixed in 10% formalin; contents were removed from stomach, duodenum and intestine and examined microscopically for type and amount.
The study used coarse ordinal abundance codes for microscopic contents rather than a modern percentage-by-volume or biomass diet estimate.
The paper separately tested bait/food attraction in a small, shallow pond. Do not conflate that experiment with the river fish gut-content observations.

growthRelatedDietChange: The author reports animal plankton and other animal food in smaller fish, including copepods, rotifers, insect larvae and the worm Limnodrilus gotoi, alongside algae and other plant material.
Across roughly 70-90 mm body length, the author describes a shift toward plant material; in fish over about 90 mm, animal food declined while plant foods, especially Spirogyra, increased.

The paper's summary characterizes adult loach as essentially herbivorous but reports temporary carnivory just after spawning. Preserve this as the author's historical site-specific interpretation, not an absolute rule for the species.
findingsAsReported.seasonality: The author reports seasonal changes in feeding time and amount, and presents selected seasonal gut-content observations for fish over 80 mm. This is not a year-round, multi-region comparison.

evidenceLimits: This is a historical study from one Japanese river and one separate pond experiment, not Philippine diet evidence, current population monitoring, or a national distribution study.
The fish were identified as M. anguillicaudatus in the paper; the repository record and reviewed methods do not provide a modern voucher, accession, or molecular identification cross-check.

The methods excerpt does not state one overall sample denominator; table observations use coarse abundance categories, so do not infer prey proportions or ranks beyond the author's stated descriptions.
Diet varied with fish size and season in this study. The adult-herbivore summary should not be generalized across all ages, habitats, seasons, or regions.
The paper does not support a Philippine prey list, local feeding claim, fish-eating behavior, fishing/bait advice, catchability, or legal guidance.

relationshipToOtherDietEvidence.assessment: The Japanese native-range study reports size-related plant/animal diet differences, while the 2014 Idaho introduced-population study reports macroinvertebrates as primary in the subset with natural stomach contents. These are different populations and methods; together they argue against treating diet as fixed, but neither determines Philippine local diet.

reuseReview.decision: Cite the article and retain only brief attributed notes. No PDF, figure, table, or transcribed gut-content data are copied into Bangwit.

nextAction: Continue toward recent native-range and Philippine diet studies with transparent sample denominators, identifiable specimens, and waterbody/season context. For Bangwit, keep any future diet claim source-specific and separate from bait recommendations.

sources.supports: Repository citation, language, access label, study dates and setting, gut-content method, size-dependent and seasonal food-habit findings.
